newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian PM suffers setback over insurance bill.
newsitem.headline: Indian PM suffers setback over insurance bill.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral suffered a setback in parliament on Wednesday when his government failed to muster enough votes to defeat an amendment barring foreign insurance firms.
Gujral abruptly withdrew a bill from the lower house of parliament when it became clear his three-month-old government did not have enough votes to defeat the opposition-backed amendment.

"We withdraw the bill," Gujral told the lower house, the Lok Sabha, after the right-wing Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) pressed for a vote on the amendment barring foreign multinational companies from the insurance sector.
Coalition partners said Gujral's government had been dealt an embarrassing setback by failing to rally enough support to push through the bill.

The bill would create the Insurance Regulatory Authority to oversee the state-controlled insurance industry, and was considered an important first step towards the eventual opening up of the sector to private competition, both Indian and foreign.

A senior Finance Ministry official said the decision to withdraw the bill sent a worrisome signal to foreign investors who were counting on the gradual opening up of India's financial services sector.
"Is this the signal we are sending to foreign investors?" the official, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said the government would put forward a new bill. "We will come back after resolving this narrow area of difference," Chidambaram told reporters after Gujral retracted the bill.
Left parties, key allies in Gujral's fractious 15-party coalition, said Gujral had suffered a humiliating setback.
"It is an embarrassment, and Chidambaram is responsible for it," said Communist Party of India leader Gurudas Dasgupta.

Earlier on Wednesday, the lower house rejected an amendment proposed by the Communist Party of India-Marxist, which is part of Gujral's coalition, to bar private firms from the insurance sector. The amendment was defeated by a 228-to-43 vote in the 545-seat house.
The government proposed in its 1997/98 (April-March) budget to open the health insurance sector to a small number of private Indian companies.
But the government was unable to rally enough supporters to defeat an amendment, proposed by the right-wing opposition BJP, which would bar multinational firms from insurance.
Instead of suffering defeat, Gujral decided to withdraw the bill.

"The attempt to invite foreign companies just like the East India Company has been foiled," BJP lawmaker Ghumanmal Lodha told Reuters, referring to the firm whose business interests in India led to two centuries of British colonial rule.
Many deputies from the Congress party, which supports Gujral but does not have any government portfolios, were out of town to attend a party meeting in the eastern city of Calcutta.
